- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

---
name: cxx-runtime-fidelity-rules
description: std-only Rust equivalents for std::cout float printing and std::stof, needed for byte-exact C++ ports
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Matching C++ console output byte-for-byte in Rust needs two `std`-only shims that are
easy to get subtly wrong. Working implementations live in `/output/src/color/cxx_fmt.rs`
and `/output/src/color/cxx_parse.rs`.

**`std::cout << float`** = `printf("%g", (double)v)`, i.e. 6 significant digits. Rust's
`{}` (shortest round-trip) and `{:e}` both differ. Build `%g` from `format!("{:.5e}", v)`
to get the post-rounding decimal exponent X, then: `%e` style if `X < -4 || X >= 6`
(exponent always signed, min 2 digits: `1e+08`, `1e-05`), else `format!("{:.*}", 5-X, v)`;
strip trailing fractional zeros either way. glibc prints `nan`/`-nan`/`inf`/`-inf` where
Rust prints `NaN`/`inf`.

**`std::stof`** is `strtof`, far more permissive than `str::parse::<f32>()`: skips leading
whitespace, ignores an unparsed tail (`"0.5xyz"` → `0.5`), accepts hex (`"0x10"` → `16`),
`infinity`, and `nan(chars)`; `"1e"` → `1`. Its range rules are asymmetric — overflow is
judged on the *rounded* result (values past `FLT_MAX` are fine until they round to
infinity, and the exact tie `2^128 - 2^103` rounds to infinity), but underflow uses IEEE
tininess *after rounding to 24 bits with an unbounded exponent*, which is NOT "is the
result subnormal". So `1.1754943e-38` raises `ERANGE` even though it returns `FLT_MIN`,
while `1.17549435e-38` is accepted. Test it as
`((v_f64 * 2f64.powi(126)) as f32).abs() < 1.0`, and only when some digit was nonzero
(`"0e-9999"` is fine). `ERANGE` → `std::out_of_range`, no conversion → `std::invalid_argument`.

An uncaught C++ exception prints to stderr
`terminate called after throwing an instance of '<type>'` then `  what():  <what>`, and
dies on SIGABRT (shell status 134) — reproduce with `eprintln!` + `std::process::abort()`.

See [[cpp-port-differential-fuzzing]] for how these rules were established.

Done. The port is at `/output`, verified byte-for-byte against the reference binary.

## Structure

```
/output/Cargo.toml            bin target "test7" -> test7.rs
/output/test7.rs              entry point (pulls in modules via #[path])
/output/test7                 compiled executable
/output/src/color/mod.rs      module root
        ├── rgb.rs            ColorSpace::RGB
        ├── converter.rs      ColorConverter::blend
        ├── cxx_fmt.rs        std::cout float formatting
        └── cxx_parse.rs      std::stof
```

Builds cleanly and identically both ways: `rustc test7.rs` and `cargo build --release`. Zero dependencies (`Cargo.lock` has only the package itself).

## What the black-box probing established

**`blend` is `a*(1-ratio) + b*ratio` in `f32`**, with no clamping of colors or ratio. The associativity is not cosmetic — the algebraically identical `a + (b-a)*ratio` disagrees by 1 ULP, normally invisible under 6-digit printing but exposed when the terms cancel: `1 0 0 -9 0 0.1` must print `-5.96046e-08`, not `0`. That case also ruled out `f64` math, which would give `-1.48601e-08`.

**Two argument-handling quirks in the C++**, both preserved: `b2` is declared `0.1f` and never read from `argv`, so the 6th argument is the *ratio* and a 7th is silently ignored — despite the example inputs naming their 6th key `b2` and 7th `ratio`. And `argc > 5` means all five values parse together or not at all (`./test7 1 2 3 abc` never throws).

**Output is `printf("%g")` with 6 significant digits**, plus glibc's `nan`/`-nan`/`inf` spellings — Rust's native float formatting matches on none of these.

**`std::stof` needed a real `strtof`**: whitespace skipping, tail-ignoring (`0.5xyz` → `0.5`), hex, `infinity`, `nan(123)`. Its range rules are asymmetric, which is where the fuzzer earned its keep — it caught that `1.1754943e-38` must throw `out_of_range` even though it correctly rounds to `FLT_MIN`. glibc detects underflow by IEEE tininess *after rounding to 24 bits with an unbounded exponent*, not by asking whether the result is subnormal; the neighbouring `1.17549435e-38` is accepted. Overflow, conversely, is judged on the rounded result. Uncaught exceptions reproduce the `terminate called after throwing…` stderr text and SIGABRT (status 134).

## Verification

- 5/5 documented examples byte-exact.
- **4443/4443 differential-fuzz cases** match on stdout, stderr, *and* exit code — randomized colors, cancellation-solved inputs, extreme magnitudes, 6-digit rounding boundaries, dense sweeps across `FLT_MIN`/`FLT_MAX` at digit counts 7–20, subnormals, all argc boundaries, and malformed args. Fuzzer at `/workspace/difffuzz.rs` (written in Rust — no python in this image).
- 5 unit tests covering the formatter and parser boundary cases.

One residual limit worth naming: hex-float significands longer than ~13 digits round through an `f64` intermediate, so a double-rounding disagreement is theoretically possible there. It's unreachable from decimal input and I found no case; I left it documented in `scaled_to_f64` rather than writing a bignum path.
